ratings.comment: Solid-state RF directly attacks the largest loss chain and is real tech (already in some products), but cost and power-level scaling for 1 kW remain hurdles.
Plausible with solid-state multi-feed, but the energy savings from removing a 5 W motor are small and it depends on solid-state sources.
Easy and effective at cutting lamp power, but the savings are tiny relative to magnetron consumption and the camera adds its own electronics.
Sensor-based cook termination is proven (sensor cook) and reduces overcooking energy, though not very radical.
Thermoelectric harvesting is creative but yields only milliwatts at low efficiency, and removing the fan would risk overheating; the net benefit is marginal.
Solid-state RF is real and directly boosts efficiency and control, though cost and the claimed 60-70% efficiency at 700 W are challenging for a consumer microwave.
Saves only a small lamp load, and a passive light pipe through a shielded door is questionable and weak in dim rooms.
Radical and relevant, but a moving conductive bulkhead changes resonance, risks arcing and RF leakage, and is mechanically hard.
Sensing-based doneness control is plausible and cuts overshoot, but is a well-known approach and not very radical.
Waveguide losses are small, and a printed ceramic slot array at kW-scale power is hard to make robust, so the efficiency gain is modest.
Solid-state RF replacing the magnetron is a real, directly efficiency-relevant substitution (GaN ovens exist), though cost is high and efficiency gains are moderate.
Saves only a tiny, intermittent lamp load, and room light piped through a fascia would be too dim to be useful, so energy impact is minimal.
Phase-array stirring is plausible with solid-state sources but needs multiple amplifiers and is only loosely tied to energy savings, and it doesn't fit well with a magnetron.
The heat-pipe recovery is technically coherent, but it adds bulk and complexity, and the heat is low grade and used only occasionally, so it is not a substitution of a part.
Using reflected power to detect doneness avoids overcooking and saves energy, but reliable inference across varied foods is hard, and it's more sensing than substitution.
GaN solid-state RF is a real, highly relevant efficiency upgrade, though already known in the industry and still costly.
Clever but the turntable motor uses ~3 W, so savings are tiny, and weak vent airflow likely can't turn a loaded platter reliably.
Passive lighting saves little (modern lamps are LEDs, and the lamp is on only during cooking), and light levels through a mesh door would be poor.
Radical idea that targets real mismatch losses, but a movable wall changes resonant modes unpredictably and adds RF-leakage and mechanical challenges.
The magnetron's waste heat is at low temperature differential, so thermoelectric recovery would be far below a third and uneconomic.
Solid-state RF is a real, researched direction with efficiency gains from variable power and no filament, though cost and actual efficiency versus magnetrons remain limiting.
Inverter microwaves already exist and are proven, so this is highly feasible and relevant but not radical.
Removing the lamp saves little energy, but IR doneness sensing is plausible and reduces overcooking, though the idea is a bit muddled.
Phased-array steering is plausible in principle but needs multiple RF sources and is costly; the turntable motor saves only a few watts.
Very radical adaptive cavity targets wasted energy directly, but moving walls with retuned resonance and sealing are mechanically and electromagnetically very hard.
Solid-state RF with higher efficiency and load-targeted power is a real, highly relevant direction, though cost and per-cell complexity are hurdles.
Thermal sensing to stop at the target temperature saves energy and is plausible, but the lamp savings are small and the substitution is partly a stretch.
The turntable motor draws only a few watts, so the energy gain is negligible, and a fan-driven air bearing is hard to make work.
Inverter-based supplies are already used in commercial microwaves, so the idea is feasible and cuts losses but is less radical.
Dosing by absorbed energy is sensible and cuts overrun, but estimating absorbed energy from reflected power is imprecise and the savings are modest.
Solid-state RF is real and efficient, with per-cell modulation matching load, though cost is high and it is not very novel, and the 'substitute cheaper' angle is weak.
Removes the turntable motor, but the motor's energy use is tiny, so efficiency gains are marginal and it depends on a solid-state array.
Ending cooking at the true done-point saves energy, but sensor-based cooking already exists and in-band permittivity sensing is hard.
Recovering magnetron waste heat is creative, but the heat is low-grade, the loop adds complexity, and the benefit is small for short cook times.
Vacuum insulation is a wild idea, but microwave cavities lose little heat in short cooks, and the cost and RF-containment challenges are high.
Real but tiny savings, since modern microwaves use LEDs or 20-25 W bulbs only briefly; camera adds cost and complexity, and the 'substitute' is cheap-ish but not simpler.
Inverter microwaves already exist, so it is feasible and efficient but not radical; the GaN/SiC claim is somewhat overreaching at 20-40 kHz.
Needs multiple solid-state sources and is costly, and the turntable motor uses negligible energy; targeted heating is the real efficiency benefit.
Waveguide losses are already small, so the gain is marginal; the probe feed is plausible but has arcing and power-handling risks.
Solid-state RF cooking is real and offers controllability and efficiency gains, though it is currently expensive and the cathode filament loss is small.
Solid-state RF raises efficiency and control, and it is real technology, but cost and thermal limits at 700 W remain hurdles.
Beam steering is a bold idea, but the saved motor power is tiny and a phased array in a cavity is costly and complex, so it is not a cheaper substitute.
Sensor-based doneness cutoff is plausible and saves energy, but existing microwaves already offer similar sensing, so it is not very novel.
Coax feeding is simpler in principle, but the waveguide's losses are already small and it is hard to keep power handling and safe isolation.
LEDs cut lamp power, which is a minor part of total energy use, and the camera adds cost and its own consumption.
Solid-state RF is real and efficiency-relevant (instant-on, no filament, better control), though GaN at ~700 W is still costly and not clearly more efficient than magnetrons.
Phased-array steering is plausible with solid-state RF and removes the motor, but the motor's draw is tiny so the energy saving is marginal; the main gain is even heating.
Reflected-power sensing is a credible way to avoid overcooking, though inferring doneness from impedance is imprecise and sensor-based cooking already exists.
Waveguide losses are already small, so the efficiency gain is minimal, and a coax probe at magnetron power is a hard engineering problem.

A cavity that shrinks to fit the load is a bold idea that targets wasted energy, but moving panels would disturb the modes and add mechanical complexity, and the claim that heating empty air is the largest loss is questionable.
A PTC ceramic susceptor tray is clever and self-limiting, but it mainly heats the surface and the claim of thawing in minutes is overstated.
Solid-state phased-array feeds are real and already exist in commercial products, and they improve uniformity, though not necessarily speed.
27 MHz RF thawing is proven industrially and penetrates deeply, but fitting it into a home cavity with electrodes is hard and runaway heating is a risk.
Sensing-based auto-defrost is feasible and useful but is already common and does not make defrosting faster.
A GaN amplifier is a plausible magnetron replacement, but it is costly and does little to speed up defrosting itself.
Solid-state RF is a real trend, and 915 MHz penetrates deeper, but the cost and the claim that it is a simple substitute are questionable; the defrost benefit is plausible.
Phase-controlled multi-feed steering is real, mainly in solid-state ovens, and it evens thawing; it does not substitute anything cheaper, though.
Reflected-power sensing of the thaw endpoint is plausible and useful, and it is already researched in solid-state ovens, but it does not speed thawing itself.
A susceptor plate that conducts heat to start melting is a clever, cheap fix for ice's low microwave absorption, though the speedup is modest and it adds heat at the surface.
Removing the waveguide is an incremental tweak, and the claimed efficiency gain is dubious since the duct loss is small and coupling affects field uniformity.
RF thawing at 27 MHz is real and effective for frozen blocks, and solid-state RF replacing the magnetron fits the SUBSTITUTE operator, though cost and shielding remain challenges.
Solid-state phased arrays are plausible and remove the turntable, but they cost more than the parts they replace and mainly improve evenness rather than thaw speed.
IR zone sensing with closed-loop power is feasible and helps even thawing, but it's not a substitution for a cheaper part and doesn't make thawing faster on its own.
Susceptor trays already exist and are easy to build, but conductive heating from below adds only modest thaw speed and the idea is not radical.
Ultrasonic thawing is real, but low-cost piezo plates can't couple enough power into air-coupled frozen food to thaw it quickly, so the claim is physically implausible.
Solid-state RF is real and enables fine continuous power control that helps gentle thawing, though it is expensive and not a cheaper substitute today.
Dielectric sensing of the ice-to-water transition is a plausible way to auto-stop defrost, though electrodes inside a microwave cavity pose practical challenges.
Susceptor trays exist and conduct heat to the underside, which helps a little, but they risk cooking or burning the contact surface and add little to deep thawing.
Electronic beam steering evens out the heating and removes moving parts, but it needs solid-state sources and the gain for defrost is moderate.
915 MHz penetrates deeper, which is genuinely useful for thawing, but the larger cavity and antenna and the cost make it a challenge for home use.
Reflected-power sensing for automatic defrost is plausible and useful, though it adds a sensor rather than substituting a part and has been explored before.
Frequency sweeping to replace the turntable is technically sound but needs a solid-state source, and it improves evenness more than speed.
A GaN solid-state source is real and under commercial development, and it gives precise power control that helps defrost, but cost is high and it is not very radical.
RF thawing at 27 MHz is proven in industrial thawing and penetrates deeply, but runaway heating and home-appliance cost and safety are challenges.
Safety is the benefit, not defrost speed, and a 48 V supply cannot drive a magnetron or deliver the needed RF power.

Solid-state RF is real and enables fine power control and even heating, but it is costly and not clearly faster at defrosting, and it is more a substitution of the source than a defrost-specific innovation.
Susceptor plates are real and heat from below, but conduction into a large ice block is slow and surface-limited, so the claim of faster centre thawing is overstated.
Sensing the ice-to-water impedance change to detect thaw is plausible, and similar sensing has been explored; it makes defrosting easier and avoids cooking, though it does not speed it up.
Fan-driven mode stirrers are a known, cheap and feasible technology that improves uniformity, but it is not novel and not specific to defrosting.

A PCM thermal battery tray is unusual, but the salt hydrate melting point and the low heat it can deliver make it slow, and charging it by microwaves is questionable, so it is unlikely to defrost quickly.
Solid-state RF is real and gives continuous power control that helps gentle thawing, though GaN amplifiers at this power are currently costly, not cheaper.
Mode stirrers are already common in microwaves and improve evenness, but this is a modest substitution that also has questionable cost savings.
Reflected-power sensing for endpoint detection is plausible and useful, but it ends thawing rather than speeding it, and it adds parts instead of being cheaper.
Package RFID tags need ecosystem adoption, and UHF tags in a microwave cavity risk damage, so it doesn't speed thawing.
Steering energy to the ice with patch antennas is interesting, but the high-power coupling, arcing and a magnetron-fed patch array make it technically doubtful.
Solid-state RF is real and plausible, and continuous power control does help defrosting, but it is expensive rather than a cheaper substitution and the thaw benefit is moderate.
Phase-steered multi-feed fields are real (solid-state RF cooking) and improve thaw uniformity, though they need solid-state sources and are not especially radical.
Sensing the thaw state through dielectric loss is sound in principle, but a floor pad is a weak coupling to food and it only stops the thaw rather than speeding it up.
This is a power-supply swap with little bearing on defrost speed, and it only makes sense alongside a solid-state RF source.
Ultrasonic heating of frozen food is a novel idea, but coupling air-to-food is poor and the heating is weak, so it is unlikely to speed thawing meaningfully.
Sensing the ice-to-water transition is plausible and directly improves defrost quality, though it is more about control than speed and is less of a substitution.
Solid-state RF with frequency sweeping is real and well specified, and it substitutes the magnetron and HV chain, though the cost is currently higher and the speed gain is modest.
Phased-array steering replaces the turntable and targets cold spots, but it needs a multi-feed solid-state source and is complex.
Burst power could speed thawing, but magnetron limits, cost, and fast thaw uniformity make it questionable, and it is more costly rather than simpler.
A tag-driven program is convenient, but it does not make defrosting faster and it depends on packaging adoption.
Solid-state RF is real and offers fine power control, but it is costly and a 50-150 W output may thaw slowly, so the gain for fast defrost is modest.
Solid-state phased-array field steering is plausible and improves uniformity, but it needs solid-state sources, so it is not a simple substitution.
Reflected-power sensing for automatic defrost is practical and helpful, though it adds sensing rather than substituting a part, and similar sensing already exists.
RF thawing at 27 MHz is proven in industry and heats thick blocks deeply, but it is hard to fit into a consumer unit and arcing is a risk.
A susceptor plate is feasible and cheap, but conductive heating from below is slow and uneven, so it helps little with fast defrosting.
Reflected power does track load changes, but mapping it to doneness across varied foods is unreliable; still a clever, concrete sensing approach.
Acoustic popcorn detection already exists in some microwaves, but extending it to sizzling and bubbling is plausible and matches how people already judge doneness.
Passive and simple, but the turntable edge temperature is only loosely coupled to food temperature and the ink may degrade or heat unevenly in a microwave.
A scent alert is wild and helps deaf users, but it signals only that cooking has ended rather than food state, and cartridge consumables and lingering smells are drawbacks.
A thermal map directly shows food readiness and cold spots, though the sub-cutoff IR window and surface-only readings add engineering challenges and the idea isn't very radical.
Listening for sizzle and boil is plausible and serves the need for feedback, though magnetron noise and the variety of foods make reliable doneness detection hard.
A door that pops open is a simple, workable tactile and visual end signal, though it adds a solenoid and may be unwelcome in some situations.

A thermal heat map shows doneness vividly, but an IR window that blocks microwaves while staying transparent is difficult, and the sensor and display are not cheaper than a bulb, so it does not really fit the SUBSTITUTE operator.

A cheap, passive colour-changing dot gives a direct per-dish readiness signal and genuinely replaces electronics with something simpler, though it only reads surface temperature and each dot is single-use.
A fibre-optic probe gives an accurate core reading and is microwave-safe, but it is costly, needs the user to insert it, and is not simpler than what it replaces.
Using reflected power to infer doneness is clever and cheap in principle, but load shifts are noisy and food-dependent so reliable doneness detection is hard.
Vent gas/humidity sensors already exist in sensor-cook microwaves, so it is plausible but not very radical; replacing the lamp is a weak substitution.
Acoustic popping detection is already used for popcorn, but the anticipatory alert is a useful feedback extension and quite feasible.
A thermochromic doneness dot is simple, cheap and directly shows readiness, though it needs a consumable sticker and has limited food coverage.
A progressive-detent knob conveys remaining time by touch, but it only reflects the timer, not the food's actual state, so it serves the need weakly.
Humidity/VOC sensing for doneness is real (sensor-cook microwaves exist), and it directly tells the user when food is ready, though it is not very radical.
Acoustic doneness detection works for popcorn and is plausible, but generalizing to other foods is hard and the microphone must survive the microwave environment.
A cheap passive thermochromic tab gives direct visual feedback and is very feasible, but it only reports surface temperature and requires a consumable.
Weighing the food to track moisture loss is plausible and elegant, but mass loss is a weak and food-dependent proxy for doneness, and the load cell must work around the microwave field.
A thermal camera viewing through the mesh gives rich, intuitive feedback, but the cost is high, and the mesh blocks infrared more than claimed, so it is only partially feasible.
Humidity/VOC end-point sensing exists in some sensor-cook microwaves, but it directly tells the user when food is actually ready.
Pitch-tracking temperature gives continuous audible progress and is simple to build, though a thermistor in a microwave cavity is awkward and the tone could annoy.
A thermochromic door heat map is imaginative, but the film can't read food surface temperature through glass and the door's metal mesh and the cavity make it implausible.
A BLE wearable alert is very feasible and useful but quite common in smart appliances and not radical.
A transparent conductive coating that doubles as an e-paper progress ring is concrete and useful, though integrating a display into the shield is challenging.
A wireless probe gives direct doneness feedback and is highly relevant, but probes already exist, and metal probes in a microwave raise safety and arcing issues.
A scent cue is a wild, non-obvious feedback channel that works without sound or sight, though cartridge cost, consumables and scent persistence are drawbacks.
A thermopile array shows surface doneness and is plausible, but it replaces the lamp rather than the signal, and it is not cheaper or simpler.
A door progress gauge is a clear at-a-glance cue, but an electrochromic panel that provides microwave shielding is costly and hard to make safe.
Acoustic doneness detection is clever and plausible for popcorn, but it is unreliable for most foods and noisy to deploy.
Passive steam film is a creative lamp substitute, but condensation on the door is a weak and unreliable readiness signal, and film durability is doubtful.
Acoustic cue sensing is plausible, and the bidirectional piezo is elegant, but fan noise and food variety make detection unreliable.
Sensing magnetron load is clever and concrete, but absorbed power changes are subtle and inconsistent across foods, so inferring doneness is shaky.
IR thermopile sensing is real and already used in some ovens, so it is feasible and relevant but not radical, and it only reads surface temperature.
A thermochromic label gives direct, clear feedback and is feasible, but it only works with labelled packaged food and adds consumable cost.
Reflected-power sensing to detect doneness is plausible and directly closes the feedback loop, though the correlation to doneness is noisy and similar to existing sensor-cook ideas.
Acoustic doneness detection is plausible for popcorn and some foods, but generalizing across foods is hard and the substitution framing of lamp replacement is loose.
Passive color feedback is simple and appealing, but the window film can't sense food temperature and would be exposed to the cavity's conditions, so it isn't plausible as described.
A scent cue for end of cooking is novel and reaches users out of earshot, but the cartridge needs consumables and the scent may not match the food or be welcome.
A printed resonator tag is inventive but metallic tags in a microwave risk arcing, and it mainly sets the target rather than telling the user when food is ready.
Humidity/VOC sensing for readiness is plausible (some microwaves already use humidity sensors) and directly gives food-state feedback, though the lamp substitution is only loosely tied.
Acoustic doneness detection is creative but unreliable, and a microphone in a microwave cavity with a sub-$0.30 classifier is unrealistic.
Outcome-based dial with sensor feedback is feasible but resembles existing sensor-cook modes and is vague on the feedback mechanism.
A clear ITO shield improves visual feedback, but ITO attenuation at microwave frequencies and durability under heat are questionable, and it only helps while the user is watching.
Phone alerts are easy and useful for remote notification but are a common connected-appliance idea, and the food state source is unspecified.
Acoustic doneness detection works well for popcorn and plausibly for some foods, but it is not general and the microwave's own noise complicates it.
Humidity/VOC sensing in the vent is already used in sensor-cook microwaves, so it is feasible and relevant but not very radical.
A passive colour cue is a creative idea, but a liner measures cavity temperature rather than food temperature, and ink degradation and microwave heating are real problems.
The scent cue is original and reaches users who cannot hear the bell, but cartridge consumables, food-specificity and cost are problems.
Using the ITO door window as a dual-role capacitive sensor is very novel, but the Faraday shielding requirements and the noisy, harsh RF environment make it hard to realise.
Solid-state RF is real and directly improves efficiency and control, though already known and costly, so it is not a cheaper substitute.
Sensor-based doneness cutoff already exists in some microwaves; it saves energy on overcooking and is easily feasible.
It saves only a small 20-25 W lamp load (LEDs already fix this), and ambient light through the door is dim and must not leak RF.
Electronic field steering is plausible with solid-state RF, but the turntable motor uses very little energy so the gain is small.
Supercapacitor buffering shifts load rather than reducing energy and adds conversion losses, cost and bulk, with questionable practicality.
Removing a 20-25 W lamp saves little energy, and the cavity would be dark in dim kitchens, but the substitution is simple and concrete.
Auto-stop on doneness directly cuts overcooking waste, but sensor fusion across varied foods and dishes is hard and the idea is not very radical.
A GaN solid-state source with load matching is a real efficiency route that also removes duty-cycling, but cost and 700 W-class maturity are barriers.
Electronic phase-steered feeds can replace the turntable and heat more evenly, but the motor's saving is small and the electronics add cost.
Recovering magnetron heat into a water reservoir is creative, but the heat is low-grade, the quantity is small, and the fan would still be needed for cooling.
Microwave lamps are typically ~20-25 W but only on during cooking, so savings are small; ambient light through a door fibre pipe would be too dim to see food well.
IR sensor cutoff is real and avoids overheating, but sensor cooking already exists and surface-only readings limit its accuracy.
Inverter microwaves are already commercial and do improve power control, though the efficiency gains are modest and the idea is not radical.
Solid-state multi-feed phase steering is real and removes the motor, but the motor's draw is tiny and solid-state RF sources are costly.
Thermoelectric recovery is creative, but at ~5% conversion efficiency it yields milliwatts at best and does not touch the main energy loss.
Replacing the lamp with a camera is plausible and saves some power, but the lamp is a minor share of total energy and a camera phone link adds standby load.
Sensor cooking already exists in commercial microwaves but does cut wasted run-time, so it is relevant and feasible, though not radical.
Solid-state RF with beamforming is a real, researched direction that improves efficiency and control, though cost and power levels remain challenges.
Heat recovery is conceptually relevant, but the magnetron's waste heat is low-grade, the household use is odd, and the heat-pipe cooling must be reliable enough to replace the fan.
An electropermanent latch is workable and cuts holding power, but the savings are tiny relative to cooking energy.
Lamp is typically on only during cooking (~20 W vs ~1000 W+ total), so the saving is small, and ambient light may be too dim, but it is a clever passive substitution.
Sensor-based cooking termination is real and saves energy, though already exists in commercial products; IR surface reading is limited for internal doneness.
Inverter microwaves are already on the market and give modest efficiency gains; feasible but not radical.
Phased-array solid-state stirring is a real research direction but requires solid-state RF sources, and the turntable motor uses little power, so the energy gain is minor.
Solid-state GaN RF is real and promising for efficiency and zone control, though cost and efficiency parity with magnetrons remain challenges.
Reflected-power sensing for auto-stop is plausible and directly improves defrost quality, though it is not very radical and does not itself speed up thawing.
Core-first heating with lossy stakes is a creative idea, but sparking risk, hygiene, and the effort of inserting the stakes make it impractical.
A passive thaw indicator helps users but does not speed up defrosting, and thermochromic ink on door glass would struggle to track food temperature.
Solid-state phased arrays give even, controllable heating and already exist in premium ovens, but cost and complexity are high and it replaces the magnetron rather than simplifying it.
Steam condensation transfers heat well and keeps food moist, but it adds a water tank and surface-wetting, and it moves away from microwave heating.

RF defrosting at 27 MHz is real and proven (e.g., NXP, Whirlpool/Miele prototypes), directly addresses fast and even thawing, though it is less novel since it exists in industry and thermal runaway remains a challenge.
Sensor-based auto-stop is highly feasible and partly exists, but it detects thaw rather than speeding it up, and is not radical.
Ultrasonic tray agitation of heavy food is implausible and in a microwave cavity is awkward, with weak effect on thaw speed.
A thermochromic window is cheap and simple, but it only informs the user and does not speed up defrosting; the temperature range and seeing food through the window are questionable.
Ohmic thawing is real, but frozen food conducts poorly, brine pouches are messy, and it is no longer a microwave, so the idea is contradictory and impractical for the home.
Practical and cheap, and some microwaves already have weight-based defrost, so it mainly avoids guesswork rather than making defrosting faster.
Closed-loop thermal control suits defrosting, but a thermistor touching food inside a microwave cavity is awkward and a surface reading may not represent the whole load.
Imaginative, but the water tray would absorb microwave energy that should go to the food, and a sealed saline tray on a turntable is messy and mismatched to different food shapes.
Cheap and passive, but it only signals progress and doesn't speed up defrosting; a film at 0 C also reads tray temperature, not food interior temperature.
Radical and directly targets speed and evenness, and solid-state RF cooking exists, but it is costly and complex and so not a cheaper substitute.
Dielectric end-of-thaw sensing is plausible and useful, but it doesn't speed defrosting and the sensing concept is fairly known.
RF thawing is real (used industrially) and suits dense blocks, but replacing the magnetron with 27 MHz plates in a home oven is costly and not simpler.
A thermochromic liner senses cavity or surface temperature rather than food temperature, so it is weakly tied to defrost speed, and it is hard to read through the door.
NFC thaw recipes are feasible and convenient, but they need packaging adoption and don't make thawing faster.
Water-bath thawing is effective, but putting water and ultrasonics in a microwave cavity is awkward, messy and not simpler, and it conflicts with the microwave heating.
RF thawing is a real, proven technology that directly speeds uniform defrost, though a consumer-priced solid-state 27 MHz unit is hard and it replaces the magnetron rather than simplifying it.
Susceptor plates are cheap and plausible, but bottom heating gives a modest speedup and the concept is fairly familiar.
Thermal imaging shows where ice remains but does not itself speed thawing, and it relies on the user to act on it.
End-point detection avoids overcooking and wasted time, but it does not speed up the defrost itself and impedance sensing in a microwave cavity is tricky.
Weight-based auto defrost is practical and cheap, though it already exists in many microwaves and is not radical.
Aroma-based doneness sensing directly tells the user when food is ready, but VOC sensors in a microwave exhaust are noisy and hard to calibrate across foods.

A colour readout of temperature on the door is intuitive feedback, but the film must survive the cavity and show food temperature through the window rather than just the glass temperature, which is doubtful.

A thermochromic glaze ring is a cheap, proven passive signal that works even after the food leaves the oven, though it indicates temperature rather than doneness and sits on the plate rather than in the microwave.
Acoustic sensing with spoken progress narration gives live feedback, but the sensing is noisy against fan and magnetron sound, and it extends beyond a simple substitution.
Weighing and IR sensing to predict the remaining time is plausible with existing components, though it is not very radical and microwave-compatible load cells need care.
VOC sensing of doneness is plausible (some ovens have humidity sensors), but aroma-based doneness is noisy across foods and the sensor drifts.
Listening for sizzle is creative, but microwave fan noise, the lack of a Maillard-type sizzle in most microwaved food, and the harsh cavity make it unreliable.
Reflected-power sensing reuses existing hardware and is physically grounded, though it is hard to map to doneness for varied foods.
A load cell is simple and feasible, and mass loss correlates with dryness, but it is a weak doneness proxy and the turntable's rotation complicates the mount.
Passive thermochromic feedback is cheap and simple, but cavity air temperature does not reflect food readiness, and the film must survive the door's mesh and heat conditions.
A passive whistle driven by the food's own steam is a cheap, clever substitution for the bell, but it only works for moist foods and the pitch would be a crude indicator of doneness.
Mass-loss tracking is a plausible, specific doneness proxy, but a load cell under a rotating plate in a microwave is awkward and the cost is higher than the part it replaces.
Smelling the food and releasing a scent cue is radical and fits the brief, but metal-oxide sensors in a hot, humid cavity and a scent cartridge are impractical and costly.
Core-temperature sensing is the most direct readiness signal, but wireless probes already exist and a probe in a microwave cavity is difficult to make safe, so it is not very novel and not cheaper.
A tempo-based buzzer with a haptic handle pulse is easy to build and inclusive, but it adds parts instead of simplifying and the tempo is only as accurate as the underlying estimate.
Acoustic doneness sensing directly tells when food is ready and is plausible for popcorn, but it is noisy and unreliable for most foods in a microwave.
A load-cell turntable gives a real progress signal, but mass loss is an imperfect proxy and the load cell must work inside a microwave cavity.
Cavity temperature colour does not indicate food readiness, and a thermochromic ring in a microwave cavity is a weak, indirect cue.
A scent cue triggered by steam is a novel, non-auditory completion signal, but scent confusion and consumable capsules limit it.
A progress ring driven by an IR sensor serves the feedback need very directly and is feasible, but it is close to existing sensor-cook features.
Humidity and VOC sensing for doneness is plausible and some existing microwaves already use humidity sensors, so it is relevant but only moderately novel.
Sonifying cooking progress as a rising pitch is novel and gives continuous feedback, though the mic must cope with magnetron noise and the pitch-to-doneness mapping is uncertain.
A thermal-haptic handle is an unusual, accessible channel, but the door handle is poorly coupled to food temperature and a hot handle is a safety concern.
Tracking mass loss with load cells is a cheap, physically grounded progress signal, though mass loss correlates imperfectly with doneness.
A thermochromic ring shows the tray's temperature rather than the food's, and the pigment degrades at high temperatures, so it is a weak proxy for readiness.
Passive thermochromic film is a clever, cheap substitute for the lamp, but door glass temperature poorly reflects food readiness and removing the lamp hurts visibility.
Sensing aroma directly targets doneness, though MOx sensors in a humid microwave cavity are tricky and it is not cheaper than a timer.
Acoustic detection works well for popcorn and is plausible, but it covers few foods and the microwave cavity is a harsh environment for a microphone.
A tactile bimetal pin is a vivid, power-free signal, but a metal pin in a microwave risks arcing and it rotates with the turntable.
A simple, feasible LED progress glow that reduces uncertainty, but it only reflects timer progress rather than real readiness, and it is more of an addition than a substitution.

Solid-state RF cooking is real and directly improves efficiency by dropping the magnetron's losses and enabling precise power control, though GaN cost and efficiency at this power level still limit it.

Electronic steering of hot spots is plausible, but it needs multiple coherent sources, which the single magnetron lacks, and the turntable motor uses only a few watts, so the energy saving is negligible.
Sensing reflected power to stop at doneness cuts wasted energy and is feasible with a directional coupler, though the doneness inference is imprecise.
A light pipe removes a small lamp load that runs only during cooking, and it is feasible, but room light is often dim and the saving is minor.
Harvesting waste heat with thermoelectrics is creative, but the small temperature difference gives negligible power and the modules would replace vents that cool the oven.

Thermochromic turntable is a clear visual cue, but it shows the tray temperature rather than the food's, it is hard to see without a lamp, and the coating faces repeated heating, washing and microwave exposure.

Easy to build and may nudge users, but it is behavioural, barely a substitution, and the energy saved is uncertain.

Passive and simple, but door glass temperature poorly reflects food temperature, and the film must survive the microwave environment and the metal mesh/shielding.
Acoustic popping detection is proven for popcorn and could extend to boiling or sizzling, though it works poorly for silent reheating.
Novel tactile feedback, but a Peltier handle is costlier than the timer it replaces, conveys little accurate food state, and is a safety concern.
Mass-loss tracking is a clever, concrete proxy for progress, but it is hard to calibrate across dishes and a rotating load cell adds cost and complexity.

A colour-changing plate is intuitive and cheap, but the ink must withstand repeated heating and washing, it reads plate temperature rather than food temperature, and it only helps if the user is looking.

Only changes perceived wait, not actual defrost speed, and the thermochromic film must survive the door environment, so it serves M4 weakly.

It saves only a small lamp load, and a light pipe through a shielded door with ambient light would give poor illumination and complicate the RF shielding.

Passive light guiding removes a small lamp load, but kitchen light is dim and the saving is trivial next to the roughly 1000 W magnetron draw.
Humidity-sensor cooking already ships in many microwaves, so it is practical and does cut waste, but it is not radical.

Inverter microwaves already exist and give modest efficiency and evenness gains, so this is feasible but not novel.
Recovering magnetron waste heat into water is creative, but the heat quantity is small and a water jacket near high voltage adds safety and complexity problems.
Acoustic sensing of popping and sizzling is plausible for some foods (popcorn) but unreliable for most, and the lamp substitution is only loosely related.

A thermochromic glaze gives an intuitive visual cue, but a ceramic turntable heats unevenly in a microwave and shows plate temperature rather than food temperature, and the glaze is hard to make durable.

Easy to build and shows progress, but a turntable's rotation does not map neatly to a printed segment ring and it adds little beyond a countdown.
A load cell measuring weight loss is a clever proxy for doneness and technically feasible, though it is fiddly in a microwave and not accurate for all foods.

Solid-state RF is a real, researched direction with better efficiency and control, though cost is high and it is not really a cheaper substitution.
Sensor-based cooking termination already exists in sensor microwaves, but it is a credible cheap substitute for a timer that avoids wasted energy.
A cost display only nudges behavior and does not reduce consumption itself; it also adds electronics rather than substituting something simpler.

Electronic phase-switched field sweeping is a real technique that removes the turntable and evens out heating, though its effect on thaw speed is modest and the cost may not drop.

Ohmic heating is a radical swap that targets the cold-core problem, but frozen food is poorly conductive at low temperature, creating runaway hot spots, electrode contact and safety problems with packaged food.

Clever use of food's own cold, but a thin pad has little thermal capacity and could even absorb microwave energy or slow thawing.

Feasible and useful for remote alerts, but a common smart-appliance feature that is neither radical nor a substitution for cost.
